title: The Colored Wall

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA says the nebula is 'basically a sunset that got ambitious!' She has taken forty screenshots! Of a window!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies the colors as ionized hydrogen and doomed romance. The first is confirmed spectrographically. The second is extrapolated from crew behavior at the viewports.
ai_flavor.rex: REX distrusts the nebula. Zero visibility, unknown contents, pretty colors. In his experience, two of those three always travel together.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes this nebula is not sponsored! An unsponsored natural wonder! CHIP is experiencing something and has filed a ticket about it!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY recommends the port viewports for the best view, and mentions — just in passing — that the last ship she served on went around. They arrived late. But they arrived.

body:
The nebula fills the forward view like a wall built by someone with strong opinions about the color teal.

The charts offer two truths: through is shorter, around is safer. Inside, sensor range drops to nearly nothing and navigation becomes a matter of feel — a phrase the manual uses with visible discomfort.

The crew has gathered at the viewports. The nebula does not care. It has been glowing for ten thousand years and will glow for ten thousand more. You are the temporary one here.

choices.text: Thread it — pilot at the helm

outcome.narrative: The pilot takes the ship through the clouds like a needle through wool — banking off density gradients, riding the clear channels, grinning the entire time in a way that would be alarming anywhere else. You emerge ahead of schedule with fuel to spare. The pilot accepts applause.

choices.text: Thread it yourself — how hard can it be

outcome.narrative: It is, as it turns out, that hard. The ship emerges from the far side trailing wisps of glowing gas and a new respect for professional certification. The hull is scuffed. The pride is scuffed worse. So is whoever was standing up when the first density wall arrived. The nebula, for its part, noticed nothing.

choices.text: Go around — the long, boring, alive way

outcome.narrative: You take the long way. The nebula slides past the viewports for more than a week, a wall of color with no opinion about your caution. The crew watches it the whole time. Somewhere in there, someone starts calling it 'the scenic route' without irony.

choices.text: Anchor at the edge and harvest gas

outcome.narrative: The gas analyzer identifies a pocket of usable hydrogen at the nebula's fringe, and the scoops drink from it for four days. Free fuel, courtesy of a cloud that has been quietly making it for ten millennia. The ship computer logs the transaction. The nebula does not invoice.

log_lore.title: GAS ANALYZER PRINTOUT
log_lore.text:
Four days of scooping, and the analyzer had time on its hands. It printed this:

THE WALL IS MOSTLY HYDROGEN. Hot young stars inside the cloud pour out ultraviolet light that strips the electrons off its atoms. When an electron falls back in, the atom gives up the energy as light of one exact colour. Hydrogen's strongest visible line is a deep red.

THE TEAL IS OXYGEN — oxygen atoms missing two electrons, glowing at a green-blue so specific that for decades astronomers thought it was a new element and called it 'nebulium.' It only shines where the gas is too thin for atoms to bump into each other. A laboratory on Earth could never make it glow like this.

THE FUEL IS YOURS. The cloud did not notice.

science_link.text: AJOY attaches a reference on why the cloud glows: starlight exciting the gas itself.
science_link.label: What makes a nebula glow

title: Something Singing

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA is humming along! She is a fifth-octave flat! She does not care! This is her best day!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the signal is electromagnetic resonance from charged gas sheets. He confirms this is the boring explanation. He has, unusually, decided not to insist on it.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has run the pattern against every known distress code, hostile beacon, and psychological warfare catalog. No matches. He remains at his post. Listening. Just listening.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has checked whether the sound is copyrighted! It predates the concept! CHIP finds this legally fascinating and spiritually troubling!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has heard this phenomenon twice before, on other ships, in other nebulas. Both crews described it the same way afterward. She won't say the way. You'll say it yourself, later.

body:
Halfway into the cloud bank, the comm array starts picking something up.

It is not a signal. The computer is firm on this: charged gas sheets discharging in rhythm, electromagnetic noise, natural, explainable, catalogued.

Run through the speakers, it sounds like singing. Not words. Not music, exactly. Something older than the difference between the two.

The crew has gone quiet. The nebula continues, unbothered, enormous, mid-song.

choices.text: Stop the ship and listen

outcome.narrative: You cut the engines. For one hour, ship time, everyone aboard sits in a metal can inside a glowing cloud and listens to gas discharge in patterns that predate their species. Nobody speaks. Afterward, nobody explains. The log entry reads 'weather delay.' The crew works differently for days — gentler, somehow.

choices.text: Record it for the xenobiologist's archive

outcome.narrative: The xenobiologist records six hours of it, annotating in real time, weeping quietly at timestamp 02:14 and denying it at timestamp 02:15. The recording joins the archive. 'Not alive,' the annotation concludes, 'but I understand why every crew asks.'

choices.text: Keep flying — schedules don't listen to clouds

outcome.narrative: You maintain speed. The singing fades behind you over the next several hours, sliding down the spectrum until it is just noise again, and then not even that. Nobody says anything. But the mess hall is quiet that night, and everyone knows what everyone else is thinking about.

science_link.text: ARIA attaches a reference: turning space data into sound is a real practice, and the results really do sing.
science_link.label: Sonification: hearing the cosmos

title: Triple Rates, As Promised

ai_flavor.aria: The rumor was TRUE! ARIA never doubted the bartender! ARIA doubted nothing!
ai_flavor.marv: A bar rumor with a positive expected value. MARV is updating several priors and enjoying none of it.
ai_flavor.rex: Survey crew confirmed non-hostile. Their coffee, however, is a war crime.
ai_flavor.chip: Triple rate confirmed! CHIP will only take the standard commission, as a treat!
ai_flavor.ajoy: Say it. Say 'the drink paid for itself.' You've earned the smugness.

body:
The survey rig is right where the bartender's rumor put it — dead in the pretty part of the nebula, instruments full, transmitter fried, three months of irreplaceable cloud data and no way to carry it home.

Their chief scientist offers you the courier contract before you finish hailing. Triple rate. Cash on transfer. The data fits in a drive the size of a sandwich.

choices.text: Take the data run

outcome.narrative: The transfer takes an hour. The gratitude takes longer. Somewhere behind you, a robot bartender is owed a very good tip.

choices.text: Do it free — science is science

outcome.narrative: The chief scientist stares at you like you've violated a law of thermodynamics. The crew walks taller for a week. The data flies home for free, which is what data always wanted.

title: Visibility Zero

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA cannot see anything! It is like flying inside a cloud! Because it is! ARIA is having a lovely time!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes that the sensors are not broken. They are simply reporting, accurately, that there is gas everywhere. He has rarely seen a more honest instrument panel.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has never flown blind into contested space. He has also never flown blind into uncontested space. He does not like either option and has prepared for both.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that collision insurance requires "reasonable visibility!" Visibility is currently zero! CHIP has filed that under "unreasonable!"
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY suggests slowing down. She will suggest it again in a minute. She will keep suggesting it until someone slows down or something else does it for us.

body:
The nebula has thickened. The viewports show nothing but a soft glow in every direction; the long-range scanners return the same smooth shrug of ionized gas whichever way they point.

Somewhere ahead there may be rocks, other ships, or nothing at all. The cloud has no opinion. It is very beautiful, and it is in the way.

choices.text: Crawl through at a quarter speed

outcome.narrative: You creep through the glow for four long days, watching the proximity alarm that never goes off. Nothing was out there. You will never be sure of that, which is the price of the slow way.

choices.text: The pilot flies it by instrument and instinct

outcome.narrative: The pilot shuts off the useless scanners, reads the ship's drift off the gas pressure on the hull, and threads the cloud like a corridor they have walked a thousand times. You come out early and slightly ahead on fuel. The pilot pretends it was nothing.

choices.text: Hold speed and trust the odds

outcome.narrative: You hold course and speed. Most of the cloud really is nothing. One part of it is a drifting chunk of something, which you meet at full speed. The hull takes it. The odds, technically, were good.

science_link.text: The ship computer files a reference: nebulae look solid from far away, but most are thinner than the best vacuum a lab on Earth can make.
science_link.label: How thin is a nebula?

title: Charge Building

ai_flavor.aria: Everyone's hair is standing up! It's like a party! A party where the walls might spark! ARIA loves a theme!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reports the hull is taking on charge from the gas at a steady rate. He has worked out when it discharges, and where. He would prefer nobody was touching anything metal at the time. Everything is metal.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has been told the threat is static electricity. He has been told several times. He continues to treat it as a boarding action, and is not wrong about the outcome.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP advises that surge damage voids the fabricator warranty! CHIP sells surge protectors! They are on the far side of the nebula!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has unplugged everything she can unplug from the bridge. She'd ground the hull and wait. Nobody likes waiting. She'd still do it.

body:
The nebula here is ionised, and the ship has been picking up its charge like a sock on a carpet. Door handles bite. The crew's hair floats. The fabricator, which is the most expensive thing aboard and knows it, has started a thin, high whine.

The charge is still building. When it goes it will go all at once, through whatever conducts best. That is usually the expensive part.

choices.text: Ground the hull and wait it out

outcome.narrative: You run the grounding line, shut the scrubbers down so they can't spark, and wait while the charge bleeds off into the gas. Four days of breathing carefully. Six points of air. Nothing arcs. Everyone's hair is back down by the third day.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} rigs a discharge spike

outcome.narrative: The engineer bolts a length of scrap to the dorsal mast, wires it to the drive and fires one short pulse to dump the charge into the gas. There is a bang like a door the size of a house. Three points of fuel. The fabricator stops whining. The engineer starts, about the spike, for days.

choices.text: Run for the edge before it peaks

outcome.narrative: You push for the far edge before the charge can peak, and nearly make it. The discharge goes through the hull, the wiring and, as feared, the fabricator, which now smells of toast and makes a new noise when it works. Six points of hull, a quarter more wear on the fabricator, and the far edge, eventually.

choices.text: Power everything down and drift

outcome.narrative: Everything that can go dark goes dark, and the ship drifts through on momentum and good intentions. Eight days in the cold with the lights off and the charge crackling quietly in the walls. Nothing burns out. Something in the crew does, a little.

title: Something in the Air

ai_flavor.aria: The ship smells like lavender! ARIA has always wanted a signature scent! She has decided this is it!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the scrubber logs. Trace nebular compounds in the cabin air, rising. He notes the crew report feeling fine. He notes that is the symptom.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has narrowed the breach to one of four seals. He cannot shoot a seal. He has inspected all four in a way that makes it clear he would like to.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that air quality is a Premium Feature! Your plan includes Standard Air! Standard Air may contain nebula! See terms!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has put the masks where everyone can find them. She isn't saying anything yet. She's just making sure they're findable.

body:
The nebula has found a seal. Nobody knows which one. The air aboard has taken on a faint violet sweetness, like a hotel lobby, and the scrubbers have begun to labour in the particular pitch the manual describes as 'advisory.'

Everyone feels fine. That is the advisory part.

choices.text: Purge the cabin air and refill

outcome.narrative: You blow the cabin air out into the nebula and refill from the reserve tanks. Fifteen points of air leave through the vents in one long violet sigh. The new air tastes of nothing at all, which everyone agrees is a great improvement.

choices.text: {crew.medic} runs masks while the scrubbers work

outcome.narrative: The medic hands out masks, sets a rota, and checks everyone's pupils every six hours whether they like it or not. Four days of breathing through rubber while the scrubbers grind the cabin clean. Six points of air. Nobody gets sick. Nobody enjoys a minute of not getting sick.

choices.text: Seal the aft decks and live forward

outcome.narrative: You seal off the aft half of the ship, galley included, and live in the front half until the leak can be found. The front half was not built for everyone. The stores left aft come back smelling of hotel lobby and go out of the airlock. Eight points of food, and some tempers.

choices.text: Suit up and find the seal from outside

outcome.narrative: Someone suits up and works along the hull, seal by seal, with a torch and a tub of sealant, until the violet stops coming in. It was the third seal. The cabin clears by morning. A little air went out with every airlock cycle, and a little plating came off with the old sealant.

title: The Storm Has an Eye

ai_flavor.aria: A storm with an EYE! ARIA has always wanted to look a storm in the eye! She's sure it will blink first!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has mapped the storm. Forty thousand kilometers across, turning. There is a calm at the center, which a pilot could reach, and a great deal of storm between here and there, which the rest of the ship would also reach.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has raised shields, set the threat level to maximum and issued a formal challenge to the storm. The storm has not responded. He considers this cowardice. He is concerned.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that ion storms are an Act of Nebula, excluded from all StellarSeal™ policies! Except Platinum! Upgrading mid-storm incurs a Mid-Storm Upgrade Fee! It is large!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has the eye on the main screen. She'd fly for it if the pilot's up to it. If not, she'd hold the shields herself. She wouldn't drift. Drifting is how ships go quiet.

body:
Ahead, the nebula is turning. A storm of charged gas the width of a small planet, rotating slowly, lit from inside by discharges that the instruments record as numbers and the eye records as a reason to look away.

It is coming this way. At its center there is a calm: a clear, still eye, on every screen. Between here and the eye is the storm.

The front has already closed in behind you. There is no going back the way you came.

choices.text: Hold the shields through it yourself

outcome.narrative: You take the shield console.

perfect.narrative: You ride the shield envelope through the front, pulsing between surges, catching every flash. Three points of hull, all of it paint. The storm passes over and goes on its way, turning, enormous, unbothered.

good.narrative: The shields hold through most of it. 'Most' does a lot of work there: twelve points of hull went in the gaps, and the dorsal sensors came back a different colour.

poor.narrative: The shields fold in the second band and the rest of the storm happens directly to the ship. Twenty-six points of hull. When it's over the crew sit in the dark for a while before anyone thinks to turn the lights back on.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} flies for the eye

outcome.narrative: The pilot dives into the storm at an angle nobody else would pick and rides the rotation in toward the center, letting the storm do half the flying. Ten points of fuel and six of hull. Then the eye: a clear, perfectly still sky a minute wide, and the pilot gives everyone the minute before flying out the far side.

choices.text: Run along the front at full burn

outcome.narrative: You turn and run along the edge of the front with everything the drive has. It is close for an hour, and then it is not. The storm keeps its course. You keep your hull. Forty percent of the fuel stays behind in the nebula as a long, bright wake.

choices.text: Cut power and let it pass over

outcome.narrative: Everything goes dark, and the storm takes four days to pass over a ship with no shields up. The discharges walk across the hull like something looking for a door. Twenty points of hull. One of you was too near a bulkhead when it arced, and is lucky that was all it did.
